display.story_text:
Thursday night at Lambeau Field, and the number says Green Bay by 3.5. I say that is a field goal and a hook of respect for a home team that has scored 144 points and allowed 145.

Here's the setup: Carolina Panthers (3-3) at Green Bay Packers (4-3), 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Prime Video, the last kickoff of the year on daylight time before the clocks fall back Sunday. The consensus has Green Bay −3.5 with a total of 47.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Carolina Panthers +3.5, Under 47.5, and a final of Packers 24, Panthers 22.

Why the Panthers? Because Green Bay hasn't separated from anybody. Seven games, 144 scored, 145 allowed, a point differential of minus one. Carolina has scored 159 and allowed 166 in six games and is 2-1 on the road. The Formula puts Green Bay at −3.5 and Carolina at −1.5, and even after handing the Packers 1.75 points for Lambeau, it comes out Carolina by 0.3. That is a coin flip wearing a field goal and a hook.

The injury report is where this game changed. Green Bay ruled out guard Travis Glover and center Sean Rhyan, so two of the men in the middle of Jordan Love's protection won't be there Thursday night. The Packers are also without linebacker Zaire Franklin, and receiver Matthew Golden is questionable. Losing two interior blockers on a short week is not how a team lays more than a field goal comfortably.

Now the honest caveat, because I don't sell sunshine: Carolina got hit too. The Panthers ruled out guard Damien Lewis, linebacker Jaelan Phillips and cornerback Akayleb Evans. Bryce Young was a full participant and started the Tampa Bay game, but he figures to face a busy night in a loud building on a short week with a patched-up front of his own, and his defense is missing a linebacker and a corner.

Why the Under? Because this Green Bay offense lives at about three touchdowns a game, 144 points in seven. The Formula's number is 47.7, and my final is 46, a point and a half shy of the posted 47.5. Two patched-up offensive fronts and two teams on four days of rest is not a recipe for fireworks. It's a recipe for punts and field goals.

The room mostly agrees with me on the side. The Formula has Panthers 25, Packers 24, an outright Carolina win, and Next Man Up has Packers 23, Panthers 22, well inside the number. Letdown Watch is the lone dissenter at Packers 25, Panthers 20, and it would happily lay the points with Green Bay. In The Trenches sits this one out, because three interior blockers are ruled out and its season numbers were built with them on the field. Follow The Money has nothing to chase: Action Network's consensus opened at Green Bay −3.5 and hasn't budged, and the total has slipped only from 48 to 47.5.

Bottom of the card: Carolina doesn't need to win at Lambeau. It needs to keep a Green Bay offense missing two interior blockers inside a field goal and a hook. That's the game I see, a one-score night decided late, with the Packers winning it and the Panthers getting the money.

games.fanatic_story:
Thursday night at Lambeau Field, 8:15 p.m. Eastern on Prime Video, the last kickoff before the clocks fall back. Carolina comes in at 3-3, Green Bay at 4-3, and both teams are on a short week. Paul Lindgren keeps the Packers' ledger of championships. Mitch Kovac reads the Panthers' depth chart like a bank statement. Somebody bring them hot cocoa, because neither one is leaving the porch.

Paul: Welcome to Lambeau, Mitch. Wipe your feet. Check the ledger: thirteen league championships. Eleven of them before the merger, and four Super Bowls, and yes, I count the two that overlap only once, so don't start.

Mitch: Thirteen. You say it like a phone number you memorized as a kid.

Paul: I did memorize it as a kid. Then I memorized the Super Bowls: I, II, XXXI and XLV. Roman numerals, Mitch. We write our history like the Senate.

Mitch: Show me the depth chart, Paul. Banners don't tackle. Carolina won the NFC South last season, and we did it the right way, from the inside out. Julius Peppers is the template: drafted here, developed here, a Hall of Famer. Homegrown defenders are the backbone of every good team this franchise has ever had.

Paul: Homegrown is lovely. So were Herb Adderley, Jerry Kramer, Willie Davis and LeRoy Butler. I can keep going until the brats get cold.

Mitch: You always do.

The season so far: Green Bay is 4-3, 2-1 at home, and has been walking a tightrope all year, 144 points scored and 145 allowed. Carolina is 3-3, 2-1 on the road, with 159 scored and 166 allowed in six games. Jordan Love started Green Bay's last game, at Detroit. Bryce Young started Carolina's, at home against Tampa Bay.

Paul: A tightrope is still a rope, Mitch, and we're still standing on it.

Mitch: By one point across seven games. That's not a ledger, Paul. That's a gas station receipt.

The matchup: Both defenses set up in a 3-4 base front. Ejiro Evero runs Carolina's, Jonathan Gannon runs Green Bay's. This week the argument starts up front, because the official injury report took a bite out of both offenses. Green Bay will be without guard Travis Glover and center Sean Rhyan. Carolina will be without guard Damien Lewis.

Mitch: Read that again, Paul. Two of the guys who snap and block for Jordan Love are out. Matt LaFleur and Adam Stenavich are going to be drawing protections on a napkin by halftime.

Paul: Napkins are for brats, Mitch. When the ground game stalls, we throw it. You've seen Lambeau in late October. The ball flies fine. Your fingers are the problem.

Then there is the rest of the report. Carolina ruled out linebacker Jaelan Phillips and cornerback Akayleb Evans. Green Bay ruled out linebacker Zaire Franklin, and receiver Matthew Golden is questionable. Bryce Young was a full participant all week, and Jordan Love isn't on the report at all.

Paul: Your guard is out too, Mitch. And your linebacker. And your corner. Our guys can count that high.

Mitch: Dan Morgan built this roster front first, Paul. Derrick Brown is still on my depth chart for a reason. We'll count, too.

For once, the injury report was fair game, and they both used it. Paul called his missing blockers a flesh wound. Mitch asked who would be snapping the ball.

Paul: Fine. Last thing. Since your first season, how many Super Bowl trophies, Mitch?

Mitch: None yet. Two NFC titles, a division banner from last year, and a building full of players we drafted ourselves. Ask me again in February.

Paul: I'll write it in pencil. The ledger only takes ink for titles.

Mitch: Keep the pencil sharp, Paul. You'll need it Thursday night.

Respect to both: a Carolina team that has played its best football away from home, a Green Bay team that cannot stop playing one-score games, and one Thursday night in the most storied building in the sport.

My call: Packers 24, Panthers 22.

display.story_text:
Two AFC heavyweights, one building in Orchard Park, and a Buffalo team that has had two weeks to think about it. Lamar Jackson is back, the number is Bills by 3, and I'm laying it anyway.

Here's the setup: Baltimore Ravens (4-3) at Buffalo Bills (5-1), 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS from Highmark Stadium, the first Sunday back on standard time. The consensus has Buffalo −3 with a total of 54.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Buffalo Bills −3, Under 54.5, and a final of Bills 29, Ravens 24.

Why the Bills? Start with the schedule. Buffalo last played in Week 6 at Las Vegas and comes in off a bye. Baltimore played Cincinnati at home last Sunday and has a normal week. The Bills are 5-1 with 197 points scored in six games, and they have been better on the road (3-0) than at home (2-1), which tells you this team travels its offense everywhere. The Formula puts Buffalo at 2.2 and Baltimore at −2, and with 1.75 for home field it comes out Bills by 6. That's a six-point team getting asked to lay only 3.

The ground game agrees. Buffalo runs for 5.4 yards a carry against a Baltimore defense that allows 3.9, and Baltimore's protection has been the shakiest thing on the field: about one sack every twelve dropbacks. Tyler Huntley started the Cincinnati game for the Ravens, but he's not the quarterback I'm handicapping. Lamar Jackson was a full participant on Wednesday's official injury report and is expected back, and Josh Allen started Buffalo's last game before the bye. The bigger Baltimore worry is on defense: Roquan Smith, Kyle Hamilton and Calais Campbell all sat out Wednesday.

Now the honest caveat. Baltimore can run too. The Ravens get 4.8 a carry against a Buffalo defense that also allows 3.9, and they are 3-1 away from home. Buffalo's rush only gets home about once every twenty-five dropbacks, so Lamar Jackson won't be running for his life. Ellen: Two weeks of rest, Owen. Joe Brady had the whole staff in the building drawing up plays while your guys were still icing their knees from Cincinnati.

Owen: Rest is nice. Hitting people is nicer. Jesse Minter and Anthony Weaver have this defense set up in a 3-4 base, and Roquan Smith sits right in the middle of it.

Ellen: We're a 3-4 base too, Owen. Jim Leonhard runs ours. Same blueprint, different zip code.

Sunday at Paycor Stadium, 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS, the first Sunday back on standard time. Tennessee comes in at 1-6. Cincinnati is 4-2. Pete Varga judges the Titans by growth, not wins, which is a handy philosophy at 1-6. Laura Kessel thinks every football question is a quarterback question, and she has the clipboard to prove it.

Laura: Pete, start with the quarterback. Always start with the quarterback. We have Joe Burrow. You have a young man named Cam Ward who started your last game against Cleveland. Discuss.

Pete: Growth, not grades, Laura. Cam Ward is the reason I wake up on Monday mornings with hope. You don't judge a rebuild by October.

Laura: I judge everything by October. October is when the quarterback shows you who he is.

Pete: Then let me show you who this franchise is. Two AFL championships, the first two ever played, back when we were the Houston Oilers. Earl Campbell. Ken Houston. Mike Munchak. George Blanda.

Laura: Three AFC titles for Cincinnati, Pete. And Anthony Muñoz, Forrest Gregg and Dick LeBeau. And Ken Riley, sixty-five career interceptions, finally voted into the Hall of Fame decades after he should have been.

Pete: Charlie Joiner.

Laura: Charlie Joiner is ours too, Pete. He's on both lists. We share him like a custody arrangement.

Pete: Then we get him on Sundays.

The season so far: Cincinnati is 4-2, 3-1 on the road, 1-1 at home, with 163 points scored and only 122 allowed in six games. Tennessee is 1-6, 0-4 at home, 1-2 on the road, with 108 scored and 156 allowed. Burrow started the Bengals' last game, at Baltimore. Ward started the Titans' last game, at home against Cleveland.

Pete: Our one win came on the road, Laura. These guys like a change of scenery.

Laura: Paycor is lovely this time of year. Bring a coat.

The matchup: Both defenses set up in a 4-3 base. Robert Saleh runs Tennessee, with Gus Bradley calling the defense and Brian Daboll calling the offense. Zac Taylor runs Cincinnati, with Al Golden on defense and Dan Pitcher on offense. Neither team runs the ball well. Cincinnati gets 3.8 yards a carry against a Tennessee defense allowing 4.4. Tennessee gets 4.0 against a Cincinnati defense allowing 4.9.

Laura: See? Everything is a quarterback question. When neither team can run, the guy throwing it decides the afternoon. Ja'Marr Chase is on my depth chart, and Joe knows where to find him.

Pete: Jeffery Simmons is on mine. And he knows where to find Joe.

That brings us to the pocket, which is where Pete gets nervous. Cincinnati's rush gets a sack about once every ten dropbacks. Tennessee's blockers give one up about once every twenty-three dropbacks, which is respectable. Tennessee's rush gets home about once every fourteen dropbacks, and Cincinnati's protection allows a sack about once every twenty-three.

Pete: Once every ten, Laura. That's a lot of knocks for a young quarterback.

Laura: Growth, not grades, Pete. Getting knocked down and getting back up is the growth part.

Pete: You've been waiting all week to use that on me.

Laura: Since Monday.

The Wednesday report is out, and the house rule still holds: stick to the sheet, no rumors. Nobody in this game has a game status yet, and both quarterbacks are clear. Ja'Marr Chase did not practice, which made Laura very quiet for about four seconds. Tyjae Spears sat out for Tennessee too.

Pete: Last thing. When Joe Burrow is your answer, what's the question?

Laura: Every question, Pete. That's the point. But even I'll admit 3.8 yards a carry means Joe has to carry the whole thing on his arm.

Respect to both: a young Tennessee team still finding itself on the road, a Cincinnati team whose defense has quietly done its job, and a November Sunday by the river where the quarterbacks get the last word.

My call: Bengals 27, Titans 18.

display.story_text:
Arizona is 2-5 and has allowed 208 points. The Cowboys are favored by a full touchdown. And I'm still taking the Cardinals, because Dallas hasn't earned the right to lay that many to anybody.

Here's the setup: Arizona Cardinals (2-5) at Dallas Cowboys (3-4), 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox from AT&T Stadium, the first Sunday back on standard time. The consensus has Dallas −7 with a total of 54.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Arizona Cardinals +7, Under 54.5, and a final of Cowboys 28, Cardinals 25.

Why the Cardinals? Because Dallas is 1-2 at home and 3-4 overall, with 189 points scored and 180 allowed. That's a losing team being treated like a contender in its own building. The Formula puts Dallas at −5.7 and Arizona at −8, adds 1.75 for home field, and comes out Cowboys by 4.1. Arizona has also been better away from home: 2-2 on the road and 0-3 in the desert.

The run defenses are the story. Both teams allow 4.9 yards a carry. Dallas runs for 4.1 and Arizona for 3.6, so neither offense is going to take full advantage, but neither defense is going to choke a game shut either. That keeps the back door open for the team getting points.

Now the honest caveat: Dallas protects its quarterback. The Cowboys have allowed a sack about once every forty dropbacks, and Arizona's rush, which gets home about once every fourteen, may not touch Dak Prescott all day. Prescott started the Philadelphia game and Jacoby Brissett started Arizona's game against Denver, and Wednesday's official injury report changes neither: the Cardinals reported no injuries at all, and the Cowboys have no game statuses yet, with George Pickens and Quinnen Williams limited. Arizona's own blockers allow a sack about once every nineteen dropbacks against a Dallas rush that gets there about once every twenty-two.

Why the Under? The posted 54.5 is a big number, and my final is 53. The Formula's number is 51.4. Both of these offenses have to go the long way, and Arizona's run game at 3.6 a carry doesn't produce quick scores. Dallas comes in on six days of rest, and Arizona flies in on a normal week. Neither side has a schedule reason to explode.

The room is unanimous on the side and split on the total. The Formula has Cowboys 28, Cardinals 24. Next Man Up has Cowboys 28, Cardinals 25, my exact score. Letdown Watch has Cowboys 28, Cardinals 22. In The Trenches has Cowboys 28, Cardinals 27 and goes Over. Every scoring opinion has Dallas winning by less than a touchdown. Follow The Money has nothing to add: Action Network's consensus spread opened at 6.5 and ticked to 7, too small a move to count, and the total hasn't moved.

Bottom of the card: I don't need Arizona to win. I need four room opinions and one stubborn set of numbers to be right that Dallas wins by less than seven. I'll take the 7.

Cowboys 28, Cardinals 25. Cardinals cover the 7. Under 54.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Sunday at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox, the first Sunday back on standard time. Arizona brings a 2-5 record. Dallas is 3-4. Neil Carver measures every Cardinals team against the club that won the NFC title in the oh-eight season, the franchise's only trip to a Super Bowl. Cole Garrison separates the Cowboys business from the Cowboys football team, and he'll tell you the business is winning.

Cole: Neil, welcome to Arlington. Look up. Take it all in. Try not to stare at the scoreboard.

Neil: Show me the comparison to the oh-eight team, Cole. That's all I ask of any Cardinals team. Does it look like the group that went to the Super Bowl? This one doesn't yet, and I'll say it before you do.

Cole: Valuation isn't a trophy, Neil. I'll say that before you do. We have five Super Bowls: VI, XII, XXVII, XXVIII and XXX. The last one was XXX, and I am painfully aware of how long ago that was.

Neil: We have two NFL championships from before the Super Bowl existed. I don't use them as proof of anything modern. But I do enjoy pointing out that Jim Thorpe is on our Hall of Fame list.

Cole: Troy Aikman, Tony Dorsett, Michael Irvin, Bob Lilly. I could fill this stadium with Hall of Famers. I just can't fill the trophy case lately.

Neil: Night Train Lane, Cole. Charley Trippi. We were playing football before you had a logo.

Cole: And Tom Landry, our first head coach, coached here for twenty-nine seasons and created the 4-3 defense everybody copied. Funny thing is, we play a 3-4 now.

That last part is technically true, and Neil enjoys it a little too much. Arizona sets up in a 4-3 base. Dallas, the franchise that gave football the 4-3, plays a 3-4.

The season so far: Dallas is 3-4, 1-2 at home and 2-2 on the road, with 189 points scored and 180 allowed. Arizona is 2-5, 0-3 at home and 2-2 on the road, with 142 scored and 208 allowed. Dak Prescott started the Cowboys' last game, at Philadelphia. Jacoby Brissett started Arizona's last game, at home against Denver.

Neil: Both of our wins came on the road, Cole. We like visiting.

Cole: You'll love it here. The parking alone is a day trip.

The matchup: Both run defenses have leaked. Each one allows 4.9 yards a carry. Dallas runs for 4.1 and Arizona runs for 3.6, so neither offense has made the most of it. In the pocket, Dallas has been a fortress, allowing a sack about once every forty dropbacks. Arizona's rush gets home about once every fourteen dropbacks, so something has to give. Arizona's blockers allow a sack about once every nineteen dropbacks, and the Dallas rush gets there about once every twenty-two.

Neil: Josh Sweat and Budda Baker are on my depth chart, Cole. They'll find a way into that fortress.

Cole: CeeDee Lamb is on mine. He finds his way into end zones. Quinnen Williams and Rashan Gary will find Brissett.

Neil: Trey McBride is the best thing on our roster. Watch him.

Cole: I'll be watching from the luxury suite, Neil. It's the business side.

The Wednesday report is out, and it gave Neil nothing to complain about: Arizona listed nobody at all. Dallas has no game statuses yet, with George Pickens and Quinnen Williams limited. Cole calls that load management. Neil calls it a start.

Neil: Last thing. Mike LaFleur, Nathaniel Hackett, Nick Rallis. Our staff is building something. What's yours building, Cole?

Cole: Brian Schottenheimer and Christian Parker are building a football team. Jerry Jones is building a brand. One of those is going very well.

Neil: Which one?

Cole: Ask me in January. If we're playing, it's both.

Respect to both: an Arizona team that plays its best football away from home, a Dallas team that can protect a quarterback with the best of them, and a Sunday afternoon beneath the roof in Arlington.

My call: Cowboys 28, Cardinals 25.

Sunday at Ford Field in Detroit, 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox, the first Sunday back on standard time. Minnesota arrives at 6-0. Detroit is 4-2 and unbeaten at home. Erik Dahl is the man who refuses to get excited about any Vikings start before January. Martin Sorensen believes in exactly one thing: that a team's window doesn't stay open forever, and Detroit's is open right now.

Martin: Erik, you're 6-0. Smile. Just once. For me.

Erik: Five games is a rumor, Martin. Six games is a slightly louder rumor. I've seen this film before. We won the NFL championship in the nineteen sixty-nine season and haven't been back to the top since. Three NFC titles in the seventies. No Super Bowl trophies. I'll smile in January.

Martin: The window is a clock, Erik. You don't wait for January. You win now, because the clock doesn't care how you feel. Detroit won four NFL championships, the last one in nineteen fifty-seven, and I am done waiting for the fifth.

Erik: Four championships, none since the Eisenhower years. And you call me the gloomy one.

Martin: Back-to-back NFC North titles, Erik. Dan Campbell turned this place around. Nobody in this building is just happy to be here anymore.

Erik: Fran Tarkenton, Paul Krause, Warren Moon. And yes, Brett Favre is on our Hall of Fame list. Don't tell the folks in Green Bay.

Martin: Lem Barney. Dutch Clark. Jack Christiansen. Old-school Lions who'd have tackled your quarterback for fun.

The season so far: Minnesota is 6-0, 3-0 at home and 3-0 on the road, with 125 points scored and only 74 allowed in six games. Detroit is 4-2, 3-0 at home and 1-2 on the road, with 184 scored and 165 allowed. Kyler Murray started the Vikings' last game, at home against Indianapolis. Jared Goff started the Lions' last game, at home against Green Bay.

Martin: Three and oh at Ford Field, Erik. We don't lose here this year.

Erik: Three and oh on the road. We don't lose anywhere. Which, again, is a rumor.

The matchup: Kevin O'Connell runs Minnesota, with Brian Flores calling a defense that sets up in a 3-4 base. Dan Campbell's Lions play a 4-3 base for Kelvin Sheppard, with Drew Petzing calling the offense. On the ground, it's dead even. Minnesota runs for 4.3 yards a carry and Detroit for 4.4, and both defenses allow 4.2.

The pocket is where it gets wild. Minnesota's rush gets a sack about once every nine dropbacks, and Detroit's blockers give one up about once every twenty-one. But Minnesota's quarterbacks have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks, and Detroit's rush gets there about once every thirteen. Both quarterbacks should bring a helmet with extra padding.

Erik: Andrew Van Ginkel and Dallas Turner on the outside, Martin. Your quarterback will see purple in his sleep.

Martin: Aidan Hutchinson will see yours first. And when Goff has a second, he's finding Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sam LaPorta and Jahmyr Gibbs.

Erik: Justin Jefferson would like a word.

Martin: Justin Jefferson can have a word. We'll have the scoreboard.

The Wednesday report is out, and Martin did not enjoy reading it. Aidan Hutchinson, Penei Sewell, Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jahmyr Gibbs all sat out Detroit's practice. Aaron Jones sat out for Minnesota. Nobody has a game status yet, and Erik was told not to gloat. He is a Vikings fan. He doesn't know how.

Erik: Last thing, Martin. If we win Sunday, it's seven games. Still a rumor.

Martin: If you win Sunday, I'm going to need a long walk by the river. The clock is ticking, Erik.

Erik: It always is. That's why I don't celebrate in November.

Respect to both: an unbeaten Minnesota defense that hasn't blinked, a Detroit team that hasn't lost at home, and a division Sunday indoors in Detroit that should come down to the last possession.

My call: Lions 23, Vikings 22.

display.story_text:
Two teams with losing records, a short number, and a Raiders team flying across the country for a 1 p.m. kickoff. I'm laying the 1.5 with the Jets.

Here's the setup: Las Vegas Raiders (3-4) at New York Jets (2-5), 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox from MetLife Stadium, the first Sunday back on standard time. The consensus has the Jets −1.5 with a total of 45.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: New York Jets −1.5, Under 45.5, and a final of Jets 24, Raiders 21.

Why the Jets? Not because of the record. New York is 2-5 and has scored 137 points in seven games. It's because Las Vegas doesn't stop anybody: 197 points allowed in seven games, and a run defense giving up 5.2 yards a carry. The Formula puts the Jets at −2.6 and the Raiders at −8.1, adds 1.75 for home field, and comes out Jets by 7.3. That's a lot of daylight for a number this short.

The ground game is where I see it. The Jets run for 3.9 a carry, nothing special, but against 5.2 allowed, that's room. Las Vegas runs for only 3.2 a carry against a Jets defense allowing 4.3. If neither team can run on the other, it's the Raiders who are in more trouble, because their defense is the one leaking.

Now the honest caveat: the Jets can't protect. New York's quarterbacks have been sacked about once every eleven dropbacks, and the Raiders' rush gets home about once every fourteen and a half. Las Vegas, meanwhile, protects well, allowing a sack about once every twenty-eight dropbacks, against a Jets rush that gets there about once every twelve. Kirk Cousins started the Raiders' last game against the Rams, and Geno Smith started the Jets' last game against Miami. Wednesday's official injury report has no game statuses yet and neither quarterback on it, so I'm going with the quarterbacks who started last week. Brock Bowers was limited for Las Vegas, and Demario Davis sat out for the Jets.

Why the Under? Because neither team runs the ball well, and offenses that can't run stall out. The Formula's number is 47.6, a little above the posted 45.5, but my final is 45. The Jets have allowed only 150 in seven games, and their defense is the best group on either side of this field.

The room disagrees about everything, which is fair for a 1.5 game. The Formula has Jets 27, Raiders 20. Letdown Watch and In The Trenches both have Jets 22, Raiders 21, a one-point Jets win that doesn't get past 1.5. Next Man Up has Raiders 24, Jets 23. Follow The Money adds nothing: the spread and total haven't moved since they opened.

Bottom of the card: a cross-country early start for a road team that can't stop the run. I'll lay the short number with the home side.

Jets 24, Raiders 21. Jets cover the 1.5. Under 45.5.

Sunday at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox, the first Sunday back on standard time. Las Vegas comes in at 3-4 after a cross-country flight. The Jets are 2-5. Vic Moreno decides what every Raiders game means by checking who's on the other sideline. Mike Lasker trusts nothing the experts agree on, and he has Super Bowl III tattooed on his heart as proof.

Vic: Who's across the field, Mike? The Jets. No offense, but this isn't the Chiefs. Nobody in Las Vegas is circling this one.

Mike: Good. The experts are usually wrong, Vic. Everybody thought we had no chance in Super Bowl III. Joe Namath said we'd win, and we won. That's the whole philosophy.

Vic: Three Super Bowls in eight seasons, Mike. XI, XV and XVIII. Jim Otto, Art Shell, Gene Upshaw, Ted Hendricks, Willie Brown. We have enough Hall of Famers to field a defense.

Mike: Curtis Martin. Don Maynard. And yes, Brett Favre played for us. He's on our list too. Everybody claims Favre.

Vic: And we've packed the vans a few times. Oakland, Los Angeles, Oakland, Las Vegas. I don't use it as an excuse. A football team is a football team wherever the stadium is.

Mike: Our stadium is in New Jersey and our name says New York. We're the last people who'll lecture you about geography.

The season so far: Las Vegas is 3-4, 1-3 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 183 points scored and 197 allowed. The Jets are 2-5, 1-2 at home and 1-3 on the road, with 137 scored and 150 allowed. Kirk Cousins started the Raiders' last game, at home against the Rams. Geno Smith started the Jets' last game, at home against Miami.

Vic: Two and one on the road, Mike. My guys like a trip.

Mike: Your guys allow 197 points. They like a trip, and so do the other team's running backs.

The matchup: Klint Kubiak runs Las Vegas, with Rob Leonard calling a defense that sets up in a 3-4 base. Aaron Glenn runs the Jets, with Brian Duker on defense in a 4-3 base and Frank Reich calling the offense. The run game is a struggle on both sides. Las Vegas runs for 3.2 yards a carry against a Jets defense allowing 4.3. The Jets run for 3.9 against a Raiders defense allowing 5.2, which is the softest number in this matchup.

In the pocket, it's a tale of two quarterbacks. The Raiders protect well, allowing a sack about once every twenty-eight dropbacks. The Jets do not, allowing one about once every eleven. The Raiders' rush gets home about once every fourteen and a half dropbacks, and the Jets' rush about once every twelve.

Vic: Maxx Crosby is going to live in your backfield, Mike.

Mike: Demario Davis and Minkah Fitzpatrick are going to make Kirk Cousins think twice about throwing the ball to Brock Bowers.

Vic: Ashton Jeanty is on my depth chart. Think about that one.

Mike: Breece Hall and Garrett Wilson are on mine. I think about them constantly.

The Wednesday report is out, and it's mostly practice-sheet stuff: no game statuses yet, no quarterback on it. Brock Bowers was limited. Demario Davis sat out for the Jets, and Breece Hall was limited. Mike says the experts will overreact. Vic says Mike is the expert.

Mike: Last thing, Vic. Everybody says this game doesn't matter. That's exactly why it will.

Vic: Everybody says that about every Jets game, Mike.

Mike: And everybody is usually wrong. Super Bowl III. Look it up.

Respect to both: a Raiders team that plays its best football on the road, a Jets defense that has kept games close all year, and a Sunday in New Jersey that only a contrarian could love.

My call: Jets 24, Raiders 21.

display.story_text:
Two 5-2 teams, both unbeaten at home, both 2-2 on the road, and a 3.5-point number in a rivalry game with a total under 40. That half point past the field goal is the whole story, and I'm taking it with Cleveland.

Here's the setup: Cleveland Browns (5-2) at Pittsburgh Steelers (5-2), 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS from Acrisure Stadium, the first Sunday back on standard time. The consensus has Pittsburgh −3.5 with a total of 39.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Cleveland Browns +3.5, Over 39.5, and a final of Steelers 22, Browns 19.

Why the Browns? Because these teams are almost the same team. The Formula puts Pittsburgh at −5.6 and Cleveland at −5.9, three tenths apart, and even with 1.75 for home field it comes out Steelers by only 2.1. In a game this tight, 3.5 is a gift. Pittsburgh has scored 153 and allowed 138 in seven games, a modest margin for a 5-2 team.

The rushes match up evenly too. Cleveland's rush gets a sack about once every thirteen dropbacks, and Pittsburgh's gets one about once every fourteen. Pittsburgh's quarterbacks go down about once every thirteen dropbacks. Nobody has a clean pocket in this game, and that tends to keep scores close.

Now the honest caveat: Cleveland's record is better than its scoreboard. The Browns have scored 133 and allowed 146, which makes 5-2 look a little lucky. Their quarterbacks have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks. And Pittsburgh runs it well, 5.0 yards a carry against a Cleveland defense allowing 4.6, while Cleveland gets 4.2 against a Steelers defense allowing 3.9. Deshaun Watson started Cleveland's last game at Tennessee, and Aaron Rodgers started Pittsburgh's last game at New Orleans. Wednesday's official injury report has no game statuses yet and neither quarterback on it. Pittsburgh's defense had a quiet practice: T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward and Jalen Ramsey all sat out. Cleveland is also on its second straight road trip.

Why the Over? This is the one total where the whole room agrees with me. The posted 39.5 is a very low number, the Formula's is 40.7, and my final adds up to 41. Pittsburgh's run game and two leaky pockets produce just enough short fields to clear it.

The room is unanimous on the Over and nearly so on the side. The Formula and In The Trenches both have Steelers 21, Browns 19. Next Man Up has Steelers 22, Browns 19, my exact score. Letdown Watch is the outlier at Steelers 23, Browns 18, the only opinion that lays the 3.5. Follow The Money stays quiet: the spread and total haven't moved since they opened.

Bottom of the card: two mirror-image teams, a Steelers win by a field goal, and a number half a point too big. I'll take it.

Steelers 22, Browns 19. Browns cover the 3.5. Over 39.5.

games.fanatic_story:
Sunday at Acrisure Stadium in Pittsburgh, 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS, the first Sunday back on standard time. Both teams are 5-2. Both are unbeaten at home. Frank Haller will remind you that Cleveland was the gold standard of professional football before the Super Bowl existed. Ed Kowalski measures every franchise by one thing: how long it keeps its people.

Frank: Look before nineteen sixty-five, Ed. Four AAFC championships in a row, then four NFL championships. Cleveland ran this league while your team was still waiting on its first title.

Ed: Noll had one job, Frank. Ever. Chuck Noll coached the Steelers for more than two decades, and it was the only head coaching job he ever had. Six Super Bowls: IX, X, XIII, XIV, XL and XLIII.

Frank: Six is a lot. I'll give you six. But I won't let anybody call Cleveland the Factory of Sadness. We had a dynasty. Look it up.

Ed: The Immaculate Reception, Frank. Fourth down, twenty-two seconds left, trailing by a point against the Raiders. And history changes forever.

Frank: You always bring that up.

Ed: Because it's the best thing that ever happened. And the Steel Curtain team in the bicentennial season started one and four, then posted five shutouts in its last nine games. Five shutouts, Frank.

Frank: Impressive. Still not eight championships.

Ed: Mel Blount. Terry Bradshaw. Alan Faneca. Dermontti Dawson. I can keep going until kickoff.

The season so far: Cleveland is 5-2, 3-0 at home and 2-2 on the road, with 133 points scored and 146 allowed. Pittsburgh is 5-2, 3-0 at home and 2-2 on the road, with 153 scored and 138 allowed. Deshaun Watson started the Browns' last game, at Tennessee. Aaron Rodgers started the Steelers' last game, at New Orleans. Cleveland makes its second straight road trip.

Ed: Your team has allowed more than it scored, Frank, and it's 5-2. That's not a dynasty. That's a lucky penny.

Frank: Wins are wins, Ed. Nobody asks how.

The matchup: Todd Monken runs Cleveland, with Mike Rutenberg calling a defense that sets up in a 4-3 base. Mike McCarthy runs Pittsburgh, with Patrick Graham calling a 3-4. Pittsburgh runs for 5.0 yards a carry against a Cleveland defense allowing 4.6. Cleveland runs for 4.2 against a Steelers defense allowing only 3.9.

The pocket is a mosh pit on both sides. Cleveland's quarterbacks have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks, and Pittsburgh's rush gets there about once every fourteen. Pittsburgh's quarterbacks go down about once every thirteen dropbacks, and Cleveland's rush gets home about once every thirteen.

Ed: T.J. Watt and Cameron Heyward, Frank. Your quarterback will hear footsteps in his sleep.

Frank: Jared Verse and Mason Graham will be visiting yours. And Denzel Ward will be waiting for anything thrown his way.

Ed: Patrick Queen in the middle. He likes this rivalry.

Frank: Everybody in Cleveland likes this rivalry, Ed. We just like it more when we win it.

The Wednesday report is out, and the editor allowed exactly one look at it. T.J. Watt, Cameron Heyward and Jalen Ramsey all sat out Pittsburgh's practice, Cleveland's Jared Verse sat out too, and nobody in this game has a game status yet.

Frank: Last thing, Ed. Mike McCarthy. How long does he get?

Ed: If he stays as long as Noll, Frank, I'll be very old and very happy.

Respect to both: two teams that have been perfect at home, two defenses that hunt quarterbacks, and an old rivalry in Pittsburgh where every yard is going to cost something.

My call: Steelers 22, Browns 19.

Sunday at Raymond James Stadium in Tampa, 1 p.m. Eastern on Fox, the first Sunday back on standard time. It's an NFC South game. Atlanta arrives at 3-4. Tampa Bay is 2-5 and still looking for its first home win. Russ Amundsen runs every Falcons opinion through the division race and nothing else. Sal Ferris wants to know who's responsible for everything, and he'll find out by Monday.

Russ: Sal, check the division, not the polls. This one counts double in my house. A division win in Tampa is worth more than any win in October against anybody from the other conference.

Sal: Who owns this, Russ? That's my question. Who owns 0-4 at home? I've got a list of names, and I'm not done writing.

Russ: Before you start firing people, remember you have two Super Bowls. XXXVII and LV. We have two NFC titles and no Lombardis, and I'm not happy about it.

Sal: Lee Roy Selmon, Russ. The first great Buccaneer. Derrick Brooks. Warren Sapp. John Lynch. Ronde Barber. We built defenses down here that people still talk about.

Russ: Deion Sanders played for us. Tony Gonzalez. Claude Humphrey. Morten Andersen kicked for us. And Brett Favre, very briefly, which nobody in Green Bay wants to discuss.

Sal: Steve Young played here too. Very briefly. We don't discuss that either.

Russ: And don't tell me about luck, Sal. You refuse to accept luck as an excuse.

Sal: Correct. Luck doesn't own anything. People own things.

The season so far: Atlanta is 3-4, 1-3 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 171 points scored and 173 allowed. Tampa Bay is 2-5, 0-4 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 162 scored and 151 allowed. Michael Penix Jr. started the Falcons' last game, at home against San Francisco. Baker Mayfield started the Bucs' last game, at Carolina.

Sal: We've allowed fewer points than we've scored, Russ. At 2-5. Explain that to me.

Russ: I can't, Sal. That's a question for whoever owns it.

The matchup: Kevin Stefanski runs Atlanta, with Jeff Ulbrich calling a defense that sets up in a 3-4 base. Todd Bowles runs Tampa Bay, also in a 3-4 base, with Zac Robinson calling the offense. Both teams run the ball well. Atlanta gets 4.9 yards a carry against a Tampa Bay defense allowing only 3.8. Tampa Bay gets 4.8 against an Atlanta defense allowing 4.1.

In the pocket, Tampa Bay has had the rougher time. Bucs quarterbacks have been sacked about once every ten dropbacks, and Atlanta's rush gets home about once every sixteen and a half. Atlanta's quarterbacks go down about once every fourteen dropbacks, and Tampa Bay's rush gets there exactly once every sixteen.

Russ: Bijan Robinson, Sal. Drake London. Kyle Pitts. Your defense can't stop all three.

Sal: Vita Vea in the middle, Russ, and Antoine Winfield Jr. behind him. And Bucky Irving and Emeka Egbuka on the other side of the ball.

Russ: Jessie Bates III will be waiting for Baker.

Sal: Baker has seen Jessie Bates before. Baker sees everybody.

The Wednesday report is out, so the house rule loosens a little. Baker Mayfield practiced fully, Emeka Egbuka was limited, and nobody in this game has a game status yet. Both men were still asked to keep their guesses to themselves.

Russ: Last thing, Sal. If we win, I'm checking the division the second the clock hits zero.

Sal: If we lose at home again, I'm checking who owns it the second the clock hits zero.

Jacksonville is rested, at home, and laying 9.5. Indianapolis is on its second straight road trip with a 2-5 record. Everything about this screams Jaguars, and I'm still taking the Colts and the points.

Here's the setup: Indianapolis Colts (2-5) at Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2), 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS from EverBank Stadium, the first Sunday back on standard time. The consensus has Jacksonville −9.5 with a total of 46.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Indianapolis Colts +9.5, Over 46.5, and a final of Jaguars 28, Colts 20.

Why the Colts? Because 9.5 is a lot to ask of an offense that has scored 154 points in six games. Jacksonville's defense has been terrific, allowing just 104, but winning by double digits takes points, and the Jaguars score about the same per game as the 2-5 Colts do. The Formula puts Jacksonville at −0.3 and Indianapolis at −6.5, adds 1.75 for home field, and comes out Jaguars by 7.9. That's a clear Jacksonville win that still falls short of 9.5.

The run game is the surprise. Indianapolis runs for 4.2 yards a carry against a Jacksonville defense allowing only 3.3, which is a tough wall, but the Colts can also hold the ball: Jacksonville runs for 4.3 against an Indianapolis defense allowing 5.1. If Jacksonville decides to grind, it burns clock, and clock is a friend to the team getting 9.5.

Now the honest caveat: the schedule. Jacksonville is coming off a bye, and Indianapolis played at Minnesota last week and now travels again. Daniel Jones started the Minnesota game for the Colts, and Trevor Lawrence started Jacksonville's last game against Houston before the bye. Indianapolis quarterbacks have been sacked about once every fourteen dropbacks, while Jacksonville's rush gets home about once every twenty-three. Jacksonville allows a sack about once every nineteen, and the Colts get one about once every seventeen. Wednesday's official injury report has no game statuses yet and neither quarterback on it. Sauce Gardner and Tyler Warren were limited for Indianapolis.

Why the Over? My final adds up to 48, over the posted 46.5. The Formula's number is 45.4, and I'm going higher because a Colts team chasing a lead has to throw, and a rested Jacksonville team should score its share in its own building.

The room is split down the middle. Next Man Up has Jaguars 27, Colts 22 and In The Trenches has Jaguars 28, Colts 21, both with Indianapolis inside the number and both going Over. The Formula has Jaguars 27, Colts 19, also inside. Letdown Watch has Jaguars 28, Colts 18 on the rest advantage. Follow The Money is the one that talks this week, and it sides with Jacksonville.

Bottom of the card: Jacksonville wins. I just don't think it wins by ten. I'll take the Colts and the 9.5.

Sunday at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, 1 p.m. Eastern on CBS, the first Sunday back on standard time. It's an AFC South game. Indianapolis comes in at 2-5 on its second straight road trip. Jacksonville is 4-2 and coming off a bye. Lou Ferraro insists the Colts are one franchise from Baltimore to Indianapolis, and he'll fight you on it. Ivy Corcoran trusts records and splits and almost nothing else.

Lou: It's one franchise, Ivy. Baltimore Colts, Indianapolis Colts. Same team. The greatest game ever played, the NFL championship in the fifty-eight season, Raymond Berry catching everything. That's our history.

Ivy: The record is the argument, Lou. Your team is 2-5. My team is 4-2. That's the whole conversation.

Lou: Three NFL championships before the merger, Ivy. Super Bowl V and Super Bowl XLI. Art Donovan. Marvin Harrison. Dwight Freeney. Eric Dickerson. Marshall Faulk. I don't start counting when the team got to Indianapolis.

Ivy: Tony Boselli. One Hall of Famer, and he's the one this franchise points to first. We're younger, Lou. We're still writing our list.

Lou: You're writing it in pencil.

Ivy: And you're writing yours in an attic.

Lou: That's fair. That one hurt.

The season so far: Jacksonville is 4-2, 3-1 at home and 1-1 on the road, with 154 points scored and just 104 allowed in six games. Indianapolis is 2-5, 1-2 at home and 1-3 on the road, with 154 scored and 180 allowed. Trevor Lawrence started the Jaguars' last game, at home against Houston before the bye. Daniel Jones started the Colts' last game, at Minnesota.

Ivy: Same points scored, Lou, and we've played one fewer game. The record is the argument.

Lou: Same points scored. I'll take it as a compliment.

The matchup: Shane Steichen runs Indianapolis, with Lou Anarumo calling a defense that sets up in a 4-3 base and Jim Bob Cooter calling the offense. Liam Coen runs Jacksonville, with Anthony Campanile calling a 4-3 and Grant Udinski calling the offense. Jacksonville's run defense is the toughest number here, allowing only 3.3 yards a carry, and the Colts run for 4.2. Jacksonville runs for 4.3 against an Indianapolis defense allowing 5.1.

In the pocket, the Colts' quarterbacks have been sacked about once every fourteen dropbacks, and Jacksonville's rush gets home about once every twenty-three. Jacksonville's blockers allow a sack about once every nineteen dropbacks, and the Colts' rush gets there about once every seventeen.

Lou: Jonathan Taylor, Ivy. He'll find a crack in that wall.

Ivy: Travon Walker and Josh Hines-Allen will find Daniel Jones first. And Travis Hunter is on my depth chart. Think about that.

Lou: DeForest Buckner and Laiatu Latu will be visiting Trevor. And Sauce Gardner will be shadowing whoever you throw it to.

Ivy: Duval will be loud, Lou. But I don't do Duval magic. I do splits.

The Wednesday report is out, and it's short on drama: no game statuses yet, no quarterback on it. Sauce Gardner and Tyler Warren were limited for Indianapolis, and Jakobi Meyers was limited for Jacksonville.

Lou: Last thing. Ivy, would you ever count the Baltimore years if you were me?

Ivy: Lou, I'd count anything that helped my argument. That's the honest answer.

Lou: Finally, a numbers person who admits it.

Respect to both: a Jacksonville defense that has allowed just 104 points in six games, an Indianapolis team still carrying one of the oldest histories in the sport, and a division Sunday in Florida where the rested team gets the first word.

My call: Jaguars 28, Colts 20.

display.story_text:
New England has been perfect at home and shaky on the road. Miami has won once all year. The Patriots are laying a full touchdown in South Florida, and I'll take the Dolphins.

Here's the setup: New England Patriots (4-3) at Miami Dolphins (1-5), 4:25 p.m. Eastern on CBS from Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, the first Sunday back on standard time. The consensus has New England −7 with a total of 44 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Miami Dolphins +7, Over 44, and a final of Patriots 26, Dolphins 20.

Why the Dolphins? Because New England's split is extreme. The Patriots are 3-0 at Gillette and 1-3 away from it. They've scored 160 and allowed 143, which is a good team, but not a team that's been blowing people out on the road. My final has New England by seven, which lands half a point short of the number.

The run game gives Miami a path. The Dolphins run for 4.7 yards a carry against a New England defense allowing 4.1, and that's the best run matchup either team has. New England runs for 4.4 against a Miami defense allowing 4.2. A Dolphins team that can run can shorten the game and keep it inside a touchdown.

Now the honest caveat, and I won't hide it: the Formula disagrees with me. It puts New England at 1.5 and Miami at −8.7, gives Miami 1.75 for home field, and still comes out Patriots by 8.5. Miami has scored 98 points in six games. The Dolphins' quarterbacks have been sacked about once every eleven dropbacks, against a Patriots rush that gets home about once every fourteen. Miami's own rush gets a sack only about once every twenty-nine and a half dropbacks. Drake Maye started New England's last game at Chicago, and Malik Willis started Miami's last game at the Jets. Both quarterbacks were full participants on Wednesday's official injury report, there are no game statuses yet, and A.J. Brown was limited for New England. New England also comes in on ten days of rest.

Why the Over? My final adds up to 46, two over the posted 44. Miami's run game should produce drives, and Maye has time to throw against a Miami rush that rarely gets home. The Formula's 42.9 is lower, which is why this one is close.

The room splits down the middle. Next Man Up has Patriots 25, Dolphins 20, and In The Trenches has Patriots 28, Dolphins 22, both with Miami inside the number and both going Over. The Formula has Patriots 26, Dolphins 17, and Letdown Watch has Patriots 25, Dolphins 17, both laying the 7 and both going Under. Follow The Money has nothing to add: Action Network's consensus spread opened at 7.5 and the total at 44.5, and each slipped only half a point.

Bottom of the card: a team that's 1-3 on the road, laying a full touchdown, against a home team that can run the ball. I'll take the 7.

games.fanatic_story:
Sunday at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, 4:25 p.m. Eastern on CBS, the first Sunday back on standard time. It's an AFC East game. New England comes in at 4-3, unbeaten at home and struggling on the road. Miami is 1-5. Glen Tolliver thinks championships are receipts for work already done, and he cares only about the next one. Carla Ruiz looks at a broken roster the way a contractor looks at a house that needs new floors.

Glen: Rings are receipts, Carla. Six Super Bowls: XXXVI, XXXVIII, XXXIX, XLIX, LI and LIII. Those are receipts. They don't win next Sunday.

Carla: Add up the rebuild, Glen. That's my whole job. Miami won Super Bowls VII and VIII back to back, and I'm proud of that. But I don't throw good years after bad decisions. Sunk costs are sunk.

Glen: I respect that. I'm the guy who refuses to get nostalgic about the dynasty. We lost Super Bowl LX to Seattle, twenty-nine to thirteen. That's the receipt I keep in my wallet.

Carla: That's a painful wallet.

Glen: John Hannah. Mike Haynes. Ty Law. Randy Moss. Curtis Martin. Fine people to have on a receipt.

Carla: Five AFC titles for Miami, Glen. Our history is real. Our present is a construction site.

The season so far: New England is 4-3, 3-0 at home and 1-3 on the road, with 160 points scored and 143 allowed. Miami is 1-5, 0-2 at home and 1-3 on the road, with 98 scored and 157 allowed in six games. Drake Maye started the Patriots' last game, at Chicago. Malik Willis started the Dolphins' last game, at the Jets.

Carla: Our one win came on the road, Glen. Home cooking hasn't helped.

Glen: Our road record hasn't helped us either. Three and oh at home, one and three away. Process says fix the road.

The matchup: Mike Vrabel runs New England, with Zak Kuhr calling a defense that sets up in a 3-4 base and Josh McDaniels calling the offense. Jeff Hafley runs Miami, with Sean Duggan on defense in a 4-3 base and Bobby Slowik calling the offense. Miami runs for 4.7 yards a carry against a Patriots defense allowing 4.1, the best ground matchup on the field. New England runs for 4.4 against a Dolphins defense allowing 4.2.

In the pocket, Miami's quarterbacks have been sacked about once every eleven dropbacks, and New England's rush gets home about once every fourteen. Miami's rush has been the quietest in this game, getting a sack about once every twenty-nine and a half dropbacks. New England's blockers allow one about once every seventeen.

Glen: Christian Gonzalez and Milton Williams, Carla. They'll make Malik Willis earn every yard.

Carla: Ollie Gordon II and Malik Washington will make your defense earn every tackle. And Zach Sieler and Jordyn Brooks will be visiting Drake Maye.

Glen: A.J. Brown and Hunter Henry will be visiting your secondary.

Carla: We've got room for guests. We're rebuilding the guest house too.

The Wednesday report is out: Drake Maye and Malik Willis both practiced fully, A.J. Brown was limited, and nobody has a game status yet.

Glen: Last thing, Carla. When does the rebuild end?

Carla: When the books balance and the scoreboard agrees, Glen. Not one day sooner.

Respect to both: a New England team with a process and a perfect home record, a Miami team whose run game can make this a fight, and a division Sunday in South Florida where the visitors have ten days of rest.

My call: Patriots 26, Dolphins 20.

Here's the setup: Philadelphia Eagles (2-5) at Washington Commanders (1-4-1), 8:20 p.m. Eastern on NBC from Northwest Stadium in Landover, the first Sunday back on standard time. The consensus has Washington −5.5 with a total of 40.5 (as of Oct 28, 6:49 p.m. ET). My card: Philadelphia Eagles +5.5, Over 40.5, and a final of Commanders 23, Eagles 22.

Why the Eagles? Because Washington is 1-1-1 at home and has scored 132 points while allowing 172 in six games. That's not a team that wins by six. The Formula puts Washington at −6 and Philadelphia at −8, adds 1.75 for home field, and comes out Commanders by 3.8. I have it closer than that, a one-point game, and 5.5 gives me plenty of room.

Washington's run game is the strongest thing on the field: 4.8 yards a carry against a Philadelphia defense allowing 4.3. That's how the Commanders win. But Philadelphia's defense hasn't been gashed everywhere, and the Eagles run for 3.9 against a Washington defense allowing 4.2, enough to stay balanced.

Now the honest caveat: the schedule and the rush. Washington last played in Week 6 at San Francisco and comes in with thirteen days of rest. Philadelphia comes in on six days of rest after hosting Dallas. And the Eagles' rush has been nearly silent, getting a sack about once every thirty-one and a half dropbacks, while Philadelphia's own quarterbacks go down about once every fourteen. Washington allows a sack about once every fifteen and gets one about once every twenty-one. Tanner McKee started the Eagles' last game, and Jayden Daniels started Washington's last game. On Wednesday's official injury report, Philadelphia listed nobody, Daniels was a full participant, Stefon Diggs sat out Washington's practice, and there are no game statuses yet.

Why the Over? This is the one where everybody in the room agrees. The posted 40.5 is low for two defenses that have allowed 175 and 172 points. The Formula's number is 46.9, and my final adds up to 45. Two leaky defenses on a Sunday night should clear it.

The room is unanimous on the Over and the Eagles. The Formula has Commanders 25, Eagles 22. Letdown Watch and In The Trenches both have Commanders 23, Eagles 21. Next Man Up has the Eagles winning outright, Eagles 23, Commanders 22. Follow The Money is the one dissent: it sides with Washington.

Bottom of the card: two teams with five wins between them, every scoring opinion inside a field goal, and 5.5 on the board. Give me the Eagles.

Commanders 23, Eagles 22. Eagles cover the 5.5. Over 40.5.
games.fanatic_story:
Sunday night at Northwest Stadium in Landover, 8:20 p.m. Eastern on NBC, the first Sunday back on standard time. It's an NFC East game. Philadelphia comes in at 2-5. Washington is 1-4-1 and coming off two weeks of rest. Ray Donnelly explains every Eagles result by watching the big men up front. Claire Benton believes coaching structure beats raw talent every time.

Ray: Watch the guards, Claire. That's where every Eagles game is won or lost. Super Bowl LIX, forty to twenty-two against Kansas City. The guards won that game, and nobody wrote it down but me.

Claire: Structure first, Ray. Joe Gibbs won three Super Bowls here, XVII, XXII and XXVI. That's what coaching does. Structure beats names on a jersey.

Ray: We have two Super Bowls too. LII and LIX. And three NFL championships before the merger.

Claire: Two NFL championships for us before the merger. Sammy Baugh. Cliff Battles. George Allen. Bobby Beathard.

Ray: Chuck Bednarik. Reggie White. Steve Van Buren. Pete Pihos. Bob Brown. Big, tough people who played up front.

Claire: Of course you'd say that.

Ray: Of course I would. And I won't take a quarterback opinion as a substitute for watching the guards. Ever.

Claire: And I won't pretend one quarterback can save a franchise without a structure around him.

The season so far: Philadelphia is 2-5, 1-3 at home and 1-2 on the road, with 127 points scored and 175 allowed. Washington is 1-4-1, 1-1-1 at home and 0-3 on the road, with 132 scored and 172 allowed in six games. Tanner McKee started the Eagles' last game, at home against Dallas. Jayden Daniels started the Commanders' last game, at San Francisco in Week 6.

Claire: Thirteen days of rest, Ray. Dan Quinn had two weeks to rebuild the structure.

Ray: Six days for us. My guards are tired. Your guards are rested. I'm already nervous.

The matchup: Both defenses set up in a 3-4 base. Nick Sirianni runs Philadelphia, with Vic Fangio on defense and Sean Mannion calling the offense. Dan Quinn runs Washington, with Daronte Jones on defense and David Blough calling the offense. Washington runs for 4.8 yards a carry against an Eagles defense allowing 4.3. Philadelphia runs for 3.9 against a Commanders defense allowing 4.2.

In the pocket, the Eagles' rush has been the quietest in the building, getting a sack about once every thirty-one and a half dropbacks. Philadelphia's quarterbacks go down about once every fourteen dropbacks. Washington's blockers allow a sack about once every fifteen, and its rush gets home about once every twenty-one.

Ray: Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, Claire. They're due. They've been due for weeks.

Claire: Daron Payne and Frankie Luvu are due too, Ray. And Terry McLaurin is always due.

Ray: Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith. And Quinyon Mitchell will be waiting for anything near McLaurin.

Claire: Jacory Croskey-Merritt is on my depth chart. Say the name three times fast and he's already in the end zone.

The Wednesday report is out. Philadelphia listed nobody. Washington had Jayden Daniels practice fully and Stefon Diggs sit out, and nobody has a game status yet. Still no guessing about who plays quarterback where, and both of them know the rule.

Ray: Last thing, Claire. If we win this, I'm giving the game ball to a guard.

Claire: If we win, Ray, I'm giving it to the play sheet.

Respect to both: two proud old franchises having hard years, a rested Washington team in its own building, and a Sunday night division game that should come down to who wins up front.

My call: Commanders 23, Eagles 22.

games.fanatic_story:
Monday night at Lumen Field in Seattle, 8:15 p.m. Eastern on ESPN on November second. Chicago comes in at 5-2. Seattle, the defending Super Bowl champion, is 4-3. Walt Brenner will remind you that professional football started with the Bears, and he means it literally. Kara Holm knows that winning a title is hard and defending one is harder.

Walt: We were here first, Kara. Eight NFL championships before the merger. Bronko Nagurski. Red Grange. We were winning titles before most of these franchises had a mascot.

Kara: Champions get hunted, Walt. We beat New England in Super Bowl LX, twenty-nine to thirteen. Every team on our schedule has that game circled. That's what a target on your back feels like.

Walt: We know a little about that. Super Bowl XX. And I refuse to let anybody tell me that team is the whole story of the Chicago Bears. We were here first.

Kara: Two Super Bowls for us, Walt. XLVIII and LX. Steve Largent. Mike McCormack.

Walt: Devin Hester. Steve McMichael. Jared Allen.

Kara: You have more Hall of Famers. We have the most recent trophy.

Walt: The most recent trophy, for now.

Kara: Exactly. Champions get hunted. I'm not assuming we repeat. Nobody should.

The season so far: Chicago is 5-2, 3-1 at home and 2-1 on the road, with 180 points scored and 143 allowed. Seattle is 4-3, 3-1 at home and 1-2 on the road, with 168 scored and only 125 allowed. Caleb Williams started the Bears' last game, at home against New England. Sam Darnold started the Seahawks' last game, at home against Kansas City.

Walt: Eleven days of rest, Kara. Ben Johnson had time to draw up something special.

Kara: Mike Macdonald had eight days, Walt. He only needs one to draw up something special.

The matchup: Ben Johnson runs Chicago, with Dennis Allen calling a defense that sets up in a 4-3 base and Press Taylor calling the offense. Mike Macdonald runs Seattle, with Aden Durde calling a 3-4 and Brian Fleury calling the offense. Seattle's run defense is the toughest number here, allowing only 3.5 yards a carry. Chicago runs for 4.4 against it. Seattle runs for 4.0 against a Bears defense allowing 4.4.

In the pocket, both rushes are busy. Chicago's gets a sack about once every eleven dropbacks, and Seattle's blockers allow one exactly once every fifteen. Seattle's rush gets home about once every thirteen dropbacks, and Chicago's quarterbacks go down about once every fifteen and a half.

Walt: Grady Jarrett and T.J. Edwards, Kara. They'll find Darnold. And Jaylon Johnson will be waiting downfield.

Kara: DeMarcus Lawrence and Leonard Williams will find Caleb first. And Devon Witherspoon will be waiting for Rome Odunze.

Walt: Colston Loveland and D'Andre Swift. We have weapons, Kara.

Kara: Jaxon Smith-Njigba would like to introduce himself to your secondary.

The Wednesday report is out, and neither team has a single name on it. We gave them their phones back. They had nothing to text.

Walt: Last thing, Kara. What does a champion owe the rest of the league?

Kara: Nothing, Walt. The rest of the league thinks we owe them a rematch every week. That's what being hunted means.

Respect to both: a Chicago team that has been one of the best stories of the year, a Seattle defense that hasn't given much to anybody, and a Monday night in Seattle where the champs have to prove it all again.

My call: Seahawks 25, Bears 20.
